summary: Link aggregation bundles several physical links between two devices into one logical link for more bandwidth and redundancy. LACP, defined in IEEE 802.1AX (formerly 802.3ad), negotiates the bundle automatically.

sections.heading: Why aggregate
bullets: More total bandwidth than a single link.
Redundancy: the bundle keeps working if a member fails.
STP sees one logical link, so no member links are blocked.

sections.heading: How LACP works
sections.body: Each side sends LACPDUs (EtherType 0x8809, slow-protocols multicast 01:80:C2:00:00:02) on every member link. They carry the system priority and MAC, a port key, and port state. Links whose partner information matches are bundled and activated; mismatches stay out. This detects misconfiguration and cabling mistakes that static bundles cannot.

sections.heading: Modes
bullets: Active: sends LACPDUs and initiates negotiation.
Passive: replies only if it receives LACPDUs; two passive ends never form a bundle.
Static ('on'): no protocol, forced bundle; risky if the peer is misconfigured.
LACPDU timing: fast (every 1 s) or slow (every 30 s).

sections.heading: Load balancing
sections.body: Frames are assigned to member links by hashing header fields so a single flow always uses the same link and stays in order. A single TCP connection therefore never exceeds one member's speed.

sections.heading: Requirements
sections.body: Members must have the same speed and duplex, belong to the same VLAN settings, and typically terminate on the same device (up to 8 active links is common).

sections.code:
interface range Gi0/1-2
 channel-group 1 mode active
interface Port-channel1
 switchport mode trunk
! verify
show etherchannel summary

sections.body: `mode=802.3ad` uses LACP; `active-backup` needs no switch support; `balance-xor` hashes statically; `balance-tlb/alb` adapt without switch cooperation.
sections.code: ip link add bond0 type bond mode 802.3ad xmit_hash_policy layer3+4

sections.body: Multi-chassis LAG presents two switches as one logical partner, so a server can aggregate links to both for switch-level redundancy. Implementations are vendor-specific (vPC, MC-LAG).

subtopics.title: Why a single flow does not speed up

sections.body: Four 1 Gb/s links give 4 Gb/s only across many flows. One file copy still caps at 1 Gb/s. Use multipath at higher layers (multipath TCP, application parallelism) to use more.

bullets: Bundle not forming: both ends passive, mismatched modes or speeds, wrong VLAN config.
Port shown as suspended or individual in the summary.
Uneven traffic: poor hash for the traffic mix; change the hash policy.

takeaways: LACP (IEEE 802.1AX) negotiates bundles with LACPDUs; at least one side must be active.
Hashing keeps each flow on one link, so a single flow is limited to one member's speed.
Members need matching speed and duplex.
MLAG extends aggregation across two switches.
